text:
Search found related 2024–2026 work, but no verified exact match combining NextItNet with a lightweight, jointly trained, from-scratch title/description encoder. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics14091748) combines item IDs with title, description and review representations, but uses pretrained BERT and a Transformer sequence backbone; its results do not establish benefits under the present data and architecture constraints. [CLA-Rec (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDM59182.2024.00032) aligns pretrained description embeddings with collaborative information, supporting task-specific alignment rather than proving from-scratch text encoding works.

Missing-text robustness has more direct evidence. [Sequential Modality Dropout (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10240) randomly removes entire modality streams during training. Across four backbones and four Amazon domains, authors report improved retention of HR@10 when text disappears; under 95% per-item missingness, retention was 61% versus 22% without dropout. These are multimodal results, not validation of a text-only NextItNet adaptation.

A plausible experiment, rather than an established finding: add shared trainable token embeddings with masked mean pooling or a small text CNN, then fuse title/description features with ID embeddings inside one NextItNet network. Preserve an ID path for missing text and train with text dropout. To distinguish semantic benefit from added capacity, compare against a parameter-matched ID-only model and shuffled item–text assignments; separately ablate titles, descriptions and missingness handling. Retrieved evidence does not establish that text resolves fine-grained product distinctions in this benchmark. Compatibility, unmet demand and simulator traits remain unobserved.
